text.p: Kingsweston, 28 Augt 1682
Dear Cousin
I have been Rouleing of late between this and Bath, and am tomorrow carrying my little fry to compliment the Company there, of which I had a coachfull of the Ladies here on Wenesday last.

So I come slow to the acknowledging yours of the 17th, which came with a valuable Cargo to me. For tho I had no concern in the subject matter of any paper you wrote, yet all of them are to me as so many modells to work by, and of like force as the five Powers in the meckanicks. Wherefore let me not want copies of what you can spare, for they shall not dye, if I or Neddy can help it.

The Prints doe constitute you one of the 3 Governors of his Majesty's Irish Revenue, but a word from your self would be more authentic. I wish for his Majesty's sake it were the worst news I could have concerning Ireland.
Rejoice at the happy arrival of your two brave Boys. Neddy will be at leisure ere long to try his cousin's patience. Happiness to all is the constant wish of
Yours
R. Southwell
London, ye 5o Sepbr 1682

Yesterday came to Town what was declared on Sunday night at Windsor, vizt, That the Revenue of Ireland is to bee managed by the Lt Longford, Lem Kingdon, one Mr Strong of the Excise, Mr Dixon of the Customs of London, and Captain Bridges of Dublin, who as tic thought did but represent Mr Trant. By good Luck I never sollicitated any body in the Case, I only putt in 3 several papers of proposals before you went hence, which I think did the service no harm. As for my self, my work hath ever been my wages in this world. My own buisnesse sticks in the Bog where you left it. I have much to say, but I have nobody to hear me.

I will review the specimen of Logic , and perhaps send it inlargd as well as explained. Wee are all in health here. Charles and his sister are in daily emulation about Arithmetic; That spirit doth begin to rise and appear in Charles upon the Charms and Conjurations of his sister. The Latin also joggs on, so as I hope you shall ere long bee ready to receive
Cousin Noddy's Arrows. As for news: it is said that the Duke of Hanover is to have my Lt Lowtherdell's Garter.

I have writ 3 sheets in answer to 31 questions concerning money. If it take (for I renounce all Judgement of my own) you shall have a Copy. But laying all these things aside, let me here that you and your family are well, for that will best please
W. P.
Kingsweston, 11 Sepr 1682
Dear Cousin

By yours of the 5th Instant I see the 5 Commissioners of the Revenue of Ireland. The first I easily guess at, but who launched the other 4 into this Bethesda I want to know? You say nothing of their Salary; nor of their subordination to the Treasury here; nor if those 2 points (which so endeared the former prosecution) doe still subsist, as to Tangiers and the Ships, wherein as a Kingsale man I am a little concerned.

But I confess I am much more, to see that when the City is delivered, yett noebody reguards the wise man. I will believe that your papers had more effect than you are told of; and seeing they turn you no better to Account, let me at least have the Transcript of what you gave in. For I shrine all up, and fancy that in after times I shall be resorted too for your works, as Mr Hedges is for the true Opo-balsamum.

I see also as to your particular affair, that you stick fast as before, and scarce know where with benefit to expose your doleance. I would advise better if I knew how; but surely it can do no hurt if you take Sir Edward Dering fresh at his arrival from Kent and explain to him that by him alone you can hope to be understood. The proposal which by my Lord Hyde's encouragement he so laboured in, being quite laid by, and new things done (wherein as being absent he has no share), I am apt to think he will not be unwilling to learn and know the extent of your case, and afterwards to act as fair opportunities shall be offered him.

I take notice that all your clouds are only without doors, for at the same time you can think and turn your mind to the instruction of the unkind world. Your 3 sheets about money shall be much more welcome to me than money itself.

And then to have the specimen of Logic enlarged, as well as explained, is a matter I really take to heart. For my chief business is now grown a solicitude for my son's education, and so I am chawing over every thing that I judge useful in order to his easier digestion. Neddy remembers you advised him to gather Tools, as Hammer, saw, pincers, gimblett &c; and he calls the arts and sciences
already by these nick-names, and means to value them no more than as they really prove such. And as he passes for the top-artisan that invents a new Tool, so Neddy means to throng in among your admirers; not only for this Logic , but for all other Tools, which either for the Sake of his cousin Charles or the Public you shall vouchsafe to frame or invent. He hopes also you will cause the 104th Psalm to be printed anew.

You have also within doors the sunshine of this new and profitable emulation between Charles and his sister. I see that tic she ferments Arithmetic in him, but how you levened her (unless ex traduce ) pray let us know. I have got Dr Wallis by the end touching this subject; for I would fine by comprehending the reason retain the practice, which else vanishes as I have found for want of frequent use.
All my young ones are well and afford me much content; tic the most sensible share of worldly happiness we can have. I doe heartily congratulate your part, and am ever Yours
R. Southwell
Kingsweston, 28 Nobr 1682.
Dear Cousin

When by yours of the 24th past I understood your putting off the evil day of a dirty and dangerous Journey, I became much more sedate than before; but when you concluded your letter with an Interdiction to your self, and such a Reverse as to say 'lett there be darknesse', I fell into grief and you may think stupidity (by my long silence); and this for many Accounts. First that the world should be so wicked as to give you provocation, but chiefly
that you should take it. For has Sir Walter Raleigh added to his character by burning half the World? Had he not been even more revenged, in heaping up coals and obleiging the ungrateful age? Besides how preposterous is it for the Iniquity of the present bystanders (which are but a handful) to bespite the inoffensive generations that are to come? And how well did Ben Johnson defy their hissings when he declared that what he had written was for Posterity. A prophet has no honour in his own time.

I have now the favour of yours of the 25th Instant, and in it some of the Rich Ore of the same old mine. Herein I first congratulate that you take home the prodigal son (I should indeed have said it of the Father) and that you let the world see plain, what they still suspected, that the spirit of Sir William Petty and not of John Grant presided in those Bills of Mortality. Poor John, tho in his purgatory, can hardly drive such points as (by your allowance) he ventured on while here, in his State of fuddling and of frailty. The good man was herein like a dwarf mounted on an Elephant.

But although, to keep gravity, you will needs excuse this new eruption and that still you are for unthinking and unobleiging too; I can but smile, as I would doe to hear natural agents such as the sun, moon, and stars talk at the same rate. Wherefore tic but weakly done to say you will not think; and tho you must think, to say you will not Ratiocinate, is to sever heate from Light, which will not doe - or to say again that though you do Ratiocinate we shall no more hear on it. You may better say so much touching Gunpowder, for tic a child when borne that cannot be murdered. Light when generated will shine out and wisdom must still cry aloud in the streets. Wherefore, dear Cousin, make a virtue of Necessity, and
what you cannot Resist or suppress, let us have it with a good Grace, and as it were, have amongst you blind Harpers.

While I was too credulous of your first anger (which yett I congratulate), I went to ransack all my papers, and have putt together in one Treasure all that ever I had from you, and which shall lye together an Heire-loom not only for this Neddy, but all the Neddyes that may come hereafter.

As to your present work; the very Pattern is Admirable - to teach men how to present to the World with vitals, and not with long Hair and Nails which commonly make up the bulk. But Cousin, this Herb is a peculiar of your own Garden, and be not angry if it springs not up in every soil. For me to attempt to propagate This method in my Neighbourhood as you propose, would be to destroy it. I am not their favourite, which I really congratulate, as much as I prefer Philosophy before drinking.
I can truly tell you that tic near a month that I wrote to Mr Dickinson and Mr John Ellis in terms of as much concern for you as I could express.
My small puggs are all well and very Jovial, for I have got them a blind Harper. I hope the like with my Godson and all his good company, being ever
Sr Your most affect Kinsman & most humble servant
Robert Southwell
I am glad you have speeded orders about our old friend Wm Fitzgerald.
Kingsweston, 16 April 1683
Dear Cousin
Your last demonstration was so killing, and in a matter of that bulk and importance, that I have remained ever since as one that had seen a miracle.

My Lord Weymouth, who is in the Role of your admirers, was lately here with me. We shall both meet by the end of this month in London, and are not to be long from your House. He was wishing he had your thoughts on the great catastrophe of Banquers; whether land will Rise, or what may be the most probable consequences thereof.

But, dear cousin, must you have had a fortunate hearing in the Treasury upon Saturday last, and must I owe the glad tidings rather to one of your Judges than your self? Well! Laus Deo , which I heartily pronounced first in consideration of Kerry, and then of nature and Philosophy. For if the World will but give you Rest, I am sure you will be Teeming.
My 3 Girls have been coughing till quite tyred out, but the approach of a London Journey seems very restorative.
With true Service to my lady, my godson, and the Rest
I am ever, Sr Your most affect Cousin & most humble servant
Robert Southwell
London, ye 19o April 1683

To yours of the 16o. I say nothing of my Demonstrations about the Growth of London. When you come, in reference to my Lord Waymouth's questions concerning Bankrupts, I will show you a scheme of a Bankrupt wherein the Lamb may wade, and the Elephant may swim &c.

I had a little opium given me on Saturday last, of which I said nothing, as doubting it might be corrected with Castorium and other strong Ingredients, - as it hath been. But I being dosd and Stupefied, can make no Judgement of it, but am sqird back like the weavers shuttle into Ireland, there to endure time and chance.

The fits of the Double-Bottome do return very fiercely upon me. I cannot bee dissuaded but that it contains most glorious, useful and pleasant things. My happiness lies in being mad. I wish I were grown up to that Degree as to believe I were fairly dealt with. I doe not attribute my wrongs to much hatred of my Person, as to other internal motions within the lucky Men of Power. Wee long here to see how wan the 3 girls will bee when they come to their cousins hither.
I am Yors
W. P.
I desire you to get me an Account of some Parishes according to the Method enclosed.
Kingsweston, 20 Sept. 1684
Dear Cousin
I had not till the last night yours of the 31st past, which I have read over and over, for the great kindness as well as variety of it.

I see the Vulture is still knowing in Kerry, when at the same time a man child is borne to make you forget that sorrow. Surely this new ship has stupefied that other anguish; and you might be exalted too much, but for that other dead weight that keeps your life in balance. In the Life of Paulus Emilius by Plutark there are these words:

"It seems the province of some God to lessen that happiness which is too great and inordinate, and so mingle the affairs of human life that no one should be entirely free and exempt from Calamities, but (as it is in Homer) that those should think themselves truly blessed to whom fortune has given an equal share of good and evil."
But as to the ship, you forget to enclose the Catalogue of wagers, which I lament. If she take into Kingrode on her way about, I will be answerable for her good reception here.

As to Kerry, I now write and lend your letter to Mr Poppies, not only for his Entertainment, but that he excite Mr Guy to all that is friendly; and in particular that Mr Dickinson may be called upon, not only to ease the Patient, but the Doctors also, who confess they know not what to make of the Case.

But I am at some stand how to think of all that
is past, and what the Reports now depending may signify, if you are (as you say) beginning all anew under the new Commission. Nor doe I hear you press on Judgment for the Reduced Column, or whether it be already done or not, whereas in this great point seemed formerly to consist your antidote to the Thunderbolt.

I would have repeated my visit to my dear Cousins in London, but that I hurried away on the sickness of my 2 eldest Daughters, who attending their Grandmother at Bath, met with this new fever which hath humbled them; For they are still but creeping towards the health and vigour which they formerly had. And this also makes our resolution of a quiet wintering in the Country the more needful, while between the Apple Roaster and the Blind Harper (who is sent for), we shall forget the long and blustering nights.

I rejoice exceedingly that my Cousin Charles is in the Career you like, and tic enough to make my Grum~ett proud that you enquire how he climbs his ropes. He is very strong; a stout rider - 110 miles in 2 days and 1/2 - going 46 the first day (when I lately sent him home from Peterbrough) all on the trott, and one day thunder and rain to the skin. He will Learn anything on Horseback, and if repeated by his Tutor, in half the time he can doe it from the book. Formerly his work was to get many of the finest passages that lay about in verse and Prose, which I reckon he will never forget, but serve hereafter as good materials when he has judgment to spinn them out. He is now chiefly intent to be absolute master of Caesar's Com~entarys, and is learning his Greek Grammar, in order to some sprinkling only of that tongue. There are Virgill's Georgics, Plutark's Lives (as newly translated) and other like things for the by. But wee are now going seriously into Arithmetic, Geometry, Astronomy and Cosmography, or some tincture or Instruction towards
them, by the help of one Ferfaix who is coming down and to stay this winter at Least amongst us.

I have never pressed or Strained on the Boy to his book, being content to let him grow att the same time in other things; which his going about with me does bring in, As an acquaintance with all my friends and the Business that is depending between us. He reads all my Letters and all the Answers I make, and sometimes he answers some for me, and will write a Letter passing well. He designs and has a Musical Voice; but when all is done, he loves play in his Heart. I have here said enough for 7 years; with all duty to my Lady and love to Charles
I am ever
Dublin, 23o Xbr. 1684
Dear Cousin

Tho I am not upon my oath, yet for the Honour of Eternal Truth, whom I have ever sought and adoard, I will tell you the whole Truth, and nothing but the Truth, concerning our Naval Experiments. Upon the 15th and 16th of this month, wee got her out, to try her sailing & c, which did not answer expectac~on. The main fault (unto which all the rest were Consequences) was not bearing sufficient Sail, which the Careening I menc~oned in my last seemed to secure our Gravest Shipwrights and Sea-men against; and is a fault the more easily remedied upon our Principle, which all our Modells do still justify. But what is all that? - Wee have suffered a Publiq disappointment!

Just now I received a joint Letter from Mr Poppies and Sir Anthony Deane, containing several wagers, with a proposal That I must bee personally a board upon all their trials; with a proposal a little before that if wee did excel all the King's yachts, that then the Charge of our Rigging should be boaren. The Considerac~on of all which doth lessen my trouble concerning this matter. I will calmly and gravely spend the remainder of my days in diging for Truth in this matter; and being conscious of no wilful miscarriage therein, will courageously endure the Reproaches and derisions of the Vulgar; remaining with my service to all of your family.
Yors most entirely
Wm Petty
London, 29th August 1685
To yours of the 25th. As to my wife's perfect Recovery, wee must have patience, but do not doubt it.

I agree with you in Hopes that the Duke of Lorraine may bee able to take down the great Troubler of the World, of whom Ireland ought to be jealous. I am also clear that if men will but consider, our terrors concerning Ireland are not well grounded. I only fear what men drunk with Rage and Revenge may doe of harm to Themselves and others.
I congratulate what you say of the pretty Spinsters and the Rest of your Rural Gazette.
I hope wee may answer your desires in the 2 Barony Maps of land near Kingsale when you come to Town.

I think there needs be no formal Essay about what I hinted for reading the Scriptures, for (1st) We hold all equally canonised. (2) Tic Manifest that St Luke and the Acts are the best History of Christ and the Apostles. (3) The Epistles of Peter, James, John and Jude, are stiled Catholiq or General Epistles, directed to the whole world, and not to Particular Churches upon special occasions. (4) They do manifestly contain the whole Christian Doctrine. I only add that the 2 Books of the Chronicles is the like Epitome of the History of the Jewish nation and Church.

What you say of My Lord Treasurer pleases me well, and I hope tic not an Embryon, but a foetus prop partum . Get but into that organ loft and I will blow your bellows, having wind enough for all your Pipes - I say Wind.

For further impositions about Neddy, I think them needless. You have planted all necessaries in his ground, you have led him through all the shops and warehouses of other things. Let nature now work. See what he will choose and learn of himself. What is cram~ed in by much teaching will never come to much, but parch away when the Teachers are gone. Within a year or two you will have a crisis on him; - let's mark that.
I am contented you will be here about the Parliament's sitting. What shall We say more, but the old assertion that I am Yours
Wm P.
Tell the spinsters what fine wool and flax I wish them to work upon, and how good a market for their wears.

I am angry that you did not speak a word, neither of Reason or Ridicule, upon the Paper for the Multiplication of Mankind ; as if that Desideratum were frivolous which I take to be equal to all the Projects which have been these many years for the advantage of the World. Pray send it back with an affidavit on the back of it That you have neither shown it to any fortunate fop, nor taken any copy of it. In dudgeon: Adieu.
Kingsweston, 5 Sept 1685
Dear Cousin

I have yours in your own ill hand of the 29th past, but what you say of my Lady's Recovery makes ample compensation. So also does your kind mention of the Spinsters, and the fair opinion of their Brother Neddy, and your Inculcateing the Method of reading the Holy Wrote, which are all favours of Weight.

But you come off at last with a Biting Postscript. You chide that I say nothing of your Calculation, as if it were so small a matter to speak Skilfully of Mankind, and to discourse in this Great Case (of) the Effects and power of Generation, as it were the putting of a dozen of Eggs under a Henn!

Your Great Demonstration is first the Defect, then the Art, and lastly the value of Multiplication . And since you will force me to object, pray answer me this: Mankind must by your method become at last as thick as grass - not 3 acres to a man, but 3 men to an acre, and what not! Nay the Sea also must be covered as far as timber can be gotten for stages and ships.

And now that I speak of a Ship, What if your proposal had been made to those on the Arck, and the Deluge were to have lasted? If getting children
had not been restrained, the Ship at last must have sunk or the Surplus gone over-board. Wherefore if the Tower you build, - how beautiful soever in the progress - must by its own height or weight fall at last, what need we raise it higher then it is?

Then your Great art cannot remain a Secret, as the Philosopher's Stone, or be monopolised by Letters Patent; for all Men are become Philosophers in this Science. And if the noise that one Kingdom (by adding a Law to Generation) is likely to Infect and devour his neighbour, be but heard, that Neighbour will presently make Resistance by the same Engine; and it will soon go about, since the practice will be more easy to the Latter than it was to the first. Yett they surely who begin with the greatest numbers will have the greatest advantage in this Experiment, tho at the last a superfetation of mankind, since our Space is Limited, must produce either Laws or Bloodshed for their necessary Reducing. So I have seen in Germany most Stately Trees for a great space Burnt down, to get a little Arable to live by. So you knew the Hebrew Children were drowned on account of Multiplication, and somewhere in Greece the old men were by Law to be tumbled over a Bridge.

Now if the Success of the Project be Ruinous, what need I speak of the Means towards it - as to putt a Girl at 16 and a Lad at 18 to get Children, before they know how to maintain them, or have served out half their Apprentiseshipps?

If a whole Country of poor Labourers should have more Children than honest labour can maintain (as may presently bee, if one may have 25 children, and the first 12 be helpless), it follows that they must be maintained by the State. And consequently the State will be owners and disposers of the Children begotten, and so introduce a vasilage which leaves the Parents no other Right to their Children than the Earth hath to its Plants. How to get new Laws and fit Judges for such a Constitution will in this our Climate be somewhat hard.

Then whereas you fix the value of a man's Labour at 83£, and so multiply the value with the increase of men, this my thinks would have a quite Contrary Effect; for if Diamonds grew as com~on as pebbles, they would be but of the same account.

So in the case of mortality, if in London it exceed that in the Country, the multiplication of other Cities will doe the like. For if there be more men, there will be and must be more communities; and the more London is populous the more will the Rule of Mortality increase. And so the future Throngs will somewhat impair the numbers you impute to the career of generac~on.

But why do I meddle in these matters? You know Calculation is not a Herb of my Garden - tic a peculiar of your own. I can only write captiously and, as they say turn the Tables', because you will have me write.

However to make you some amends. I will conclude with a story: There is a Province in China where by the constitution, all of the com~on sort who desired to marry, were twice a year to send up their names to the Capital City and to some Senators who presided for That End. Six of these took Care of the Males, and six more of the Females, and at the day of appearance each of the numbers were marshalled into 3 Squadrons. The men into the most Rich, the most Poor, and those who were indifferent. Also the women into the most Fair, the most ugly, and those also who were indifferent. These indifferents were matched up on equal terms. The most beautiful were at high and valuable rates paid for by the most Rich; and at last the most Poor married the most Ugly. Yett they had this satisfaction: to have all the money divided among them which the most rich had given for the most fair. After this the magistrates lead them to the Nuptial
House, where at the public charges they had fiddles and sack possett for that night, and the next morning they had leave to depart.
I have shown your Paper to Mr Poppies, who is but one of all mankind who are concerned in it; And I doe hereby make affidavit that I have taken a copy of it.
Yrs
R. S.
Kingsweston, 24 Sept 1685
Dear Cousin

The Enclosed is to one part of your kind letter of the 19th. As to the other, about the Irish Settlement, I must have a little time to ruminate on those master Strokes you give, which in the mean time I very heartily thank you for.
I use my servant's hand in the Enclosed, because you have complained that my own is not always current.

I hope my lady and the little ones are as I wish them. Mine here I thank God are so. Neddy briggs of your Favours and the fine Maps he has in custody. My 2 daughters think they have got all the mathematics because they can demonstrate an equilateral Triangle.
Neddy has got from Caspar a clear plain Stile in all his Letters, so that I never have one hard word from him, which I am pleased with.
I have nothing more to add concerning Hobby Horses, and therefore remain
Sr, Your most affect Kinsman & humble served
Robert Southwell
London, 10 October 1685
Dear Cousin

Let me tack on a tip to the tail of our Multiplication business. I have yours of the 24th past. I have out of it and all your other letters picked out what properly belongs to that matter. I have out of my first garble again picked out what was wit, ornament, and Raillery, from the rest. In which finding (tho good) objections against what was not in my first essay, I have added such matter to the Essay as is a fit anvil for your heavy homers. That what you have ingeniously written may not bee lost, I have made men to bee kilt by your Arms. And all this I am importuned to print, wherefore make hast up hither. To conclude (Cousin), If I
find that you have done me or my Essay any harm, I will satisfy my Justice upon you only by telling all the women of between 16 and 41 years old that you hinder their having husbands &c. Concerning the Quaeries , Let the Devil take them for me.

In consequence of what I said to Monsr Paschall's paper, you would have me do by dear Neddye's head as my Lady Duchess of Ormond did to the round tower in Kilkenny; that is make his wall thiner, break out Lights, make partitions, set up Shelves, bring in furniture, new Frame the stairs, make new passages &c. To all which I will make no answer till you come. I see tic better and easier to bee banged or beaten by you, than to write anything that pleases you.

Nevertheless to begin the furnishing of Neddyes Tower, I send you the shortest Catechism I can frame, and suitable to our Com~on prayer Catechism. I call it Religio Christiana puerilis - I might ad Et quae etiam est mea senilis .

Here is come out a book of note A Papist misrepresented and represented written by J. L. I object that Hee ought to have put nothing in his Column of 'Misrepresented', but what is found in authentic non-papist authors; and nothing into his Column of 'Represented' but the very words of the Council of Trent. So have you this mighty book answered. When you come up, I will show you 2 sheets written by W P. to the said purpose.
I do not know what you meant by 'Brewing' - Explain it, and your operations upon Kings-Weston.
Adieu
W. P.
Kingsweston, 31 Oct. 1685
Dear Cousin

Although I am preparing by this day Seven-night to kiss your hand, yett in the mean time I will thank you for your last, and the Character therein of your short Cathechisme, which I annex also to the Text and send it now to our Neddy to doe the like.

Whatever enemy you think me to Multiplication , I have this day planted above 40 fair Trees, and I hope they will produce their like, and so on in Secula Seculorum . O that I could but help to plant one Cedar in Kerry, and have the same prospect of duration! But how my Charity or Courage shall avail herein, unless you have some white powder or other, that can putt any man forward like a Prince Credential! Doe but you take care of this part and I'll warrant you for following Instructions.
I long to see the pretty Governante and our Fingallian upon the Stage. My 3 Spinsters charge me strictly to bring them down an exact account of all performance therein.

I see you allow me when I come up to talk of stuffing out our puccane I mean Neddy. One point I resolve shall be to know whether you ever wrote down a Set of Cases in the way of Political
Arithmetic, in order to instruct and settle the present Age in the method, for this you once did Intend.
I hope my lady is in perfect health and all the little ones. Mine are merry and content, which is as good as being wise.
I am ever, Sr, Your most affect & most humble servant
Robert Southwell
Kingsweston, 23. Dec 1685
Dear Cousin
Our Neddy is come, and what between him and Christmas, the Girls think they may be romps by authority. Tic only Mr Kneller that keeps them to any rules of proportion.

Your 3 Papers that he brought me, and your letter - the mother that wrapped them all - are welcome more than Christmas it self. I must say as old Dr Clayton, that you brought 3 quarters of these things into the world with you. Non vox hominum sonat. Your Branches of Regal authority show all the extent of that magnificent Palace at once.
Your judgment about the Art of Sweetening Sea Water makes me but wish that I had a list of all those thoughts and estimates which produced those few but effectual and mighty determinations.
The Epigrams and Mottoes on that Subject show what numberless thoughts you have had, and a method how to employ the Chipps, after you have hewed out the Mayne Timbers and beams for use.

The two stratagems of Arithmetic in your letter are very pleasing to us. We admire at the hidden affinity that lies in numbers, and breaks out as water that runs sometimes underground and sometimes
above. This I say in reference to the second trick about scattered numbers and their Totals. As to the first, by placing the digits 15 just is made in 6 places, but more in the other 2 places.

These matters were the more seasonable for that we had already plungd into a french book of Mathematical Revelations, and poor Noddy's head was almost cloven by hard questions which the girls had prepared for him. They are now reconciled, and all of them your votaries; and doe pay all duty to my Lady, and wish all manner of happiness to their Cousins.
I have my share in all these things, and will, as the time requires, conclude with a happy Christmas to you; and am ever with great acknowledgements Your most affect kinsman & most humble servant
Robert Southwell
Kingsweston, 28 April 1686
Dear Cousin

It is strange I should be so long in acknowledging yours of the 8th, but there are things to tell you of. I was since then at Badminton to meet my Lord of Ormonde - I was at Bathe to compliment my Lord Tirconnell - and at Longleat to bid farewell to my Lord Weymouth, who goes not so soon as he pretended. I have had also some ill tricks of my sore throat: and even your letter was sick, for all of that post fell into the River and yours was tattered and torn, and it was almost Algebra to find it out.

After this sincere preamble, I will as sincerely answer you as I can, for what you write concerns your self and 3 cousins whom I have reason to esteem. I say your self, because you mention the Explanation of 12 Theological Words . I am afraid you may herein Quiet mover , and so blister your fingers; and if you show them at all to any, I wish you would let me have the first sight. You know I am your Saucy friend, and adventer to chide while others choose to accuse.
As to Cousin Charles, I like extremely the Scope of his Travel. You point at several useful enterprises, but say all in saying he is to shift among the dangerous men.

For his mimicall faculty I am as much at a plunge as if my son were a great dancer on the High Rope. If there were no falling in the case, the vigour and activity would be pleasing enough! You handle the matter so as to disown and applaud it at once. You think it is a good offensive weapon and yett such an one as may need a sword to defend It. You think it will allure women, although it terrify men. And so you pass to say that his sister hath a dash of the same. Now I should be sorry to pervert the Observation; and that any she-friend of mine should either terrify women or allure men - Nor can there be a sword in this case to defend it!

Can you not remember a certain lady of the Land, who for acting others in her Chamber was brought upon the public Stage, and Sempronia was punished more at once than all the Secret farces were worth. Tic true, in mere Children any Simptome of Wit is welcome; but as to my cousin Ann that is now taking her ply, root this weed out I conjure you, as you would a piece of Witch Craft!

I have been told of a Marshall of France, Monsr Clerambaut, who was wont to say "Queen est maestro du Ridicule est maestro du monte" ; and that the Duke of Buckingham was so in Love with this saying and that man's example, that he resolved to build upon the same foundation. Build he did (as you very well know), but the foundation being nought, the Storms and tempests beat down his House and great was the fall thereof.

As to my Cousin Harry, I am extremely in Love with his faculty of Pro and Con , for that will certainly bring in guinyes at Westminster Hall, tho he should never comprehend whether Pro or Con were most in the Right. This I say because I knew a great man that fulfilled It.

I will advise our Neddy to strict in with Cousin Harry betimes, and to Steal a Sight of all the little and great Instructions you give to become picklock of the Law. We have no other engine at present but the demonstrations of Euclide.
I pay all service to my lady and kindness to the little ones, being ever Sr, Yrs
RS.
Kingsweston, 29 May 1686
Dear Cousin

I had your condoling Letter of the 22nd, and pray allow me to tell you what my Little daughter said, being a while ago full of mirth and good humour at the Discourse that was between us: "Truly father", said she, "If a dog should come into the Room, you doe say such play things, that I believe you would make him Laugh."

Cousin, you doe wipe off Tears at a very strange rate, but why did nature furnish Them if there must be no Sorrow? Can you, by pointing at what is contemptible in a noble object, Establish your maxim in this also: That nothing is Stronger than its weakest part? I should rather say it is unnatural to lessen any thing that is either anihilated, or must rise glorious. For tho your friends in Eutopia triumph and sing Hymns at a Funeral, tic but to fortify those that must Dye, and by this disguise fling sugar into the bitter Cup. If you would know nature's mind, see what is done even by the men of Leest Humanity. The Cafras and Hattintoes never loose a Friend or Relation but they cut off a Joint from one of their Fingers - so much they scorn the acquisition of Mourning Rings. The Indian women burn with their dead Husbands, And the Husbands of Angola appoint when they dye who shall for 8 days Console the afflicted Widow, and it falls to their next of kin thus to cohabit with Her if they dye Intestate.
Funus justa petit and Sal liquefied ut condiat . Tears are the true and natural balsam, and they who refuse Them rob the Dead.

But what Art - I was going to say play-words - does your kindness find out to stifle my resentments? You tell me of Empire, and how much I assend by the desolations that are past. If by loosing one wife I have Title to the million that are unmarried, by the same right your million have Title to me; which would prove but a hard Chapter. And how can you magnify my Headship over Infants by the loose of Sir John Percivale? Is not this to magnify the Rolling of Sysiphus's stone - to begin again at the Bottom when I was at the Mountain's top, and thought I had nursed up those who in reason should turn nurses to mine?

Thus you see, Cousin, I will not be comforted. For while your good nature finds Arts to divert Sorrow, It discovers there is some sorrow due; and it being as debt, the soonest payment will be the best.

As to the Ship, you have already had my wandering thoughts. I doe for Consolation sometimes read the Chapter, how there arose a tempestuous wind called "Euroclidon"; yett after all, how some by swimming, others on Boards and broken planks, got all to Land, so as not a soul was lost. In the next place, when I am more shaken, and think where Neddy (The Pinnace) may have surest anchorage in omne eventum , I start up and shape his Course, blow high, blow low, towards Westminster Hall; for whatever happens Crafty Knaves will Live.
I am Yrs
R. S.
Kingsweston, 7 June 1686
Dear Cousin

I have the favour of 2 of yours of the 5th and the 'State of a Case' Enclosed. One of your Letters is upon Death without Mourning , and seeing it is hard to defend passion against Reason, I will acquiesce in your Arguments and read them upon ill accidents, in hopes they will support me.
As to the State of the Case you send now, and the State you sent before, I cannot think how any Cases can be more strong that are not of Mathematical Demonstration.

Nor did I tell you what I happened to over hear, but with most friendly Intention - that you might look early out. I have known you formerly to mind your Cylinders, while your Acres were Tearing from you; and you would not desist from Philosophy, as long as it was not in the power of a Decree to forbid Rubarb and Cena from purging.

But since the discovery of my own fears hath exceeded all due proportion and that you send "Hulchy Pulchy" to defy It; I will take heart also, as did your Boy Thom, who was sorely affrighted at the roaring of the Sea and the trembling of the Vessel, till he heard the seamen swear.

I am glad you expect better things from the new, than you felt from the old Council, and I had no meaning in that phrase of "Land in the Moon" but to excite you as aforesaid. For mariners doe usually cry 'all hands Aboard' when there is thoughts of any danger.

I hope, Cousin, in the mean time it will be no false Latin to look well after my Hay, or if I go on with my new Invention of an Oxe-House, where the Cattle are both to eat and drink in the same Crib, and not to stir till they be fitted for the Slaughter. Magister Arts Venture
I am ever yrs
R. S.
Piccadilly, 12 Junii 1686
Dre Cozn

To yours of the 7th I return this humble long answer. I beg your pardon (1o) for comparing your friendly warnings to Goblins and Devils, (2o) for seeming to defy them all with the spell of 'hulchi' &c, wherein I did not doe well. Pray doe not punish me by supposing the like hereafter, for I took all very kindly and thankfully.

Nevertheless what shall a man say who hath been used like me ( e.g. in Kerry), but at some times and to an Intimate friend use some words of contempt and desperation when Right and Reason will doe no good? What I said to you was but like that of Rhubarb &c. to the Court of Claims. And I am glad that my spell 'Hulchi' gave you the same comfort that the Seaman's swearing did to Tom.

Among other weapons that I am scouring up, I have drawn out a paper showing what money I had at Xmas 1636 - which was 1s. How it rise to 4s 6d, then to 24s, then to 4£. Then to 70. Next how it fell to 26, then rise to £480 at my Landing in Ireland. Next to 13,060£ at finishing the Survey. And how after I got my Land in Ireland and Estate in England &c, it was 3200£ at the King's Restoration &c. And so all along to this very day. Perhaps the like hath not been seen. This and the like gave me courage wherewith I fought Zanchy. Whatever becomes of me I can leave such arguments of 50 years art and Industry as will be a credit to my children
and friends. And now instead of Hulchi Pulchi I say God's Will be done - Naked came I into the World and naked must go out of it.'

I did, Dear Cozen, obtrude upon you the Case with Lord Dunsany and obeyed you in sending that of Tegrohan. I take my turn to obtrude again upon you that of Macgillicuddy which I think must needs come upon the Stage. And then you shall command another, and so as long as you please, but no longer.

Enlarge a little upon the Meat and Drink Cribs which you have for your Oxen. I envy you rural contentments - give me an alms out of your abundance. Fear not Neddy; Isle warrant hee will live, your Godson is short of him in that faculty,
Adieu
Kingsweston, 10 July 1686
Dear Cousin

Here has been a great Irish wedding in our neighbourhood, and by the title I took share in it, and part of the dinn has even reached this poor place. And these are the causes why I come thus slow to acknowledge yours of the 12th past.

I am now returning to the care of Hay Harvest and of my Oxe-House. In this there is nothing new, but that a Stream of Water is to run under the Crib, so they drink where they stand and when they please; and this want of Liberty is to hasten them for the Slaughter. If Irish Rents come in no better, I must invent something more - either the art of fasting or Monsr Payim's Invention to soften beans.
I perceive you are scouring old papers, and your short hint of Meliorations from the year 1636 is so entertaining that I wish I had more of It.

I thank you for the State of McGillocuddy's business which I have now read again, and I think your measure is very hard, but the time now to redress it much harder. For who can mind right or wrong touching Ham~ocks and Cabins when the whole Ship is in danger, or lies at Hull? And yett I am told (tho you say nothing of It) that Sir William Petty had great access to the Great Man before his going over; that he gave him in several Schemes as to Adventurers and Soldiers, and urged so well the preference of Money to any disturbance of the present Settlement, that the Great Man himself seems to have a Bias that way; that he has been heard to say how his own Fortune was settled by the Acts, and that His Majesty has no thought of parting with a foot of his estate in that Country. And this is all I can say as to the Mayne.
I am glad you fancy that Neddy will find out the way of shifting among dangerous men. It will import him both for his own sake and his sisters too.
I hope my good lady and all yours are well. We have lost in Sir William Coventry a great man of our nation.
I am ever ire
R. S.
Piccadilly, 13 July 1686
Dr Cozen
I will now answer but a small part of yours of the 10th Instant, and divide even that small part into the 3 partites following (1) Concerning myself. (2) Neddy. (3) The great man you mention.

Concerning Myself, I say that I had 13,060£ in cash anno 1656, which at 10 per cent (above 12 being then justly taken) would anno 1666 have been 26,120£, and anno 1676 52,240£, and in this year 1686 104 thousand 480£. I further say that, without meddling with forfeited lands, I could Anno 1656 have returned into England and been at the top of practice in Oliver's Court, when Dr Willis was casting waters at Abington Markett and the Cock Lower but an Egg. And what the superlucration thereof (besides the 104m £) might have been in 30 years, I leave to your judgment. I say the profitt of these 2 funds, would have exceeded my present State by .

As to Neddy, I say that this present great and early acquaintance, with the easy access to great Men, will give him bread and cheese by the Law before he bee ripe; whereas my Harry may be an able man 7 years before he gets bread only.

As to the Great man, I had indeed strange access and acceptance. I spake unto him as one having authority and not as the Scribes and Pharisees. I said several sour things which he took as Juice of Orange Squeezed into his Mince meat, and not as Vitriol. For some of the things he told me were these:
1o. That all the Lands which the Irish lost as forfeited were not worth Anno 1653, when they left them, near 300m pounds.

2o. That the 34,000 men which the heads of the Irish were permitted and assisted to carry to foreign States, at 10£ per head, were worth more than the said Lands; but 10£ is not 1/2 the value of negroes nor 1/5 of Algier slaves, nor 1/7 of their real value in Ireland.
3o. I said that what the Irish got restored Anno 1663, more then what belonged to them Anno 1641, is now worth much more than all they ever lost.

4o. That they got 1100m Acres of Land by Innocence, making 7 of 8 Innocent. Whereas it appears by the arrears allowed to the 49 officers, that there was a Protestant Army of 20m men from 1641 to 1649, which army together with the 7/8 of the Irish that were Innocent, could not beat 1/8 nocent part of the Irish, but necessitated my Lord of Ormond to make the Peace of 1648 - vide the Articles.

This (as Sir Jerome said) "was not half". He heard me with trouble and admiration. He pressed me to speak of the Settlement. I told him there were things in it against the light of Nature and the current Equity of the World, but whether it was worth the breaking I doubted; but if It were broken by Parliament I offered things to be mixed with those Acts as should mend the Condition of all men.
Thus much for the present from him who is Yours
W-P.

The next shall be how I got the shilling at Xmas 1636. How I came by 4s 6d when I went to sea and how I advanced the same to 24s when I went to the Jesuits College. What the setting of my Broken Leg cost to the farrier's wife, what for Crutches &c.
Kingsweston, 11 Augt 1686
Dear Cousin

I have yours of the 7th and am so conscious of my late silence, that you deal hardly with me to reproach it. You have sung so many new and surprising Tunes that I am just like the Cobbler's Daw - struck mute on the Caesurean Triumph. But, as in a month he burst out with all the music he had heard, so I wish I may prove like that Daw in this part.

We have been of late wholly Intent on our friends from Ireland, and on Sunday the last parcel arrived. And I have frequent returns of a Scurvy Soar Throat, so that, unless I would only admire , I am not in a condition to speak to you at large.

Tic almost 20 years past that I have desired the
explanation of Ut Apes Geometriam , and you may judge if I am not exalted now to see so many master strokes thereon, and more perhaps than ever you thought at First. But tic now a cloudy and a rainy day, and I will not risk or execute what Tully says on such occasions - periclitandae sunt verse ingenii, et ista mantis interna comentatio proferenda est - for I cannot yett think as I ought or utter what I think. So this is only to bespeak your patience and to advise you to look well after your flock, since already your spinster is called upon. I expect no such humours till Irish Rents are better paid, or to pay Goats Hair instead of wool.

My Lady Percivale does most thankfully acknowledge yours and my ladies kind remembrances. She has here 2 brave brawny boys as loud as bedlams and the Girl is of the same Tribe; and in November we expect an other of the same Scantling.
I am ever Yrs
R. S.
Kingsweston, 13 Sept 1686
Dear Cousin

I have yours of the 9th and the Essay Enclosed therein. If admiration could please you I can afford very good measure, but if you love Victory more than submission, I must displease you for I am not able to contend. I have read the paper with strange delight, and doubtless so will the Pope, for my thinks that King should hold none of his Councils secret while a blind man in London can describe more of his Condition that he knew himself. In the mean time you have done our King great Honour to show the world that he Governs the greatest City that is in it.

When I consider this discourse and your others of like Nature, let me putt you in mind how you have formerly promised a Sort of Gram~ar or Instruction whereby this Age may be enabled to calculate as you have done, and which assuredly was never done before. Our Neddyes head might in time take this Bias, for he is Inclined to Numbers.

What shall I add more at present save my thanks for your great favour in this precious Token, and to one who is already so much in arreare to you upon other Accounts. I still beg for time. And if in the mean time you know what the great Lord is doing, and to what end Mr Nagle, the great Surveyor of Ireland, is come over with him, you will be so kind as to impart a word unto
Yrs
R. S.
All services from herein to the Lady and the little ones.
Dear Cousin

We stand in need of your Judgment in a material point. A certain wayfaring man called the other day, and taking notice that one of the 3 spinsters had a very browne neck, "Child" said he "you will not get a Husband unless your neck look whiter" - "Sir" said she "by the time I need a Husband, Browne Necks may come into fashion" - "No" said he "I will here present you with an Amber Neck-lace which will gain you favour immediately; but once that it is on, you must never take it off" - "No Sir" said she "perhaps I may live so long as that such a neck lace may come to throttle me at last." Now what think you of the Girle's Answer?

I read lately a melancholy prophesy, and the
contents were much to my own sense, and the prophet was a Great Caldean, and had long conversed with Men and Stars; so as I was much disquieted thereat. But when I considered that these things were not wrote either in Serious Prose or in broken ejaculations or distracted words, but in smooth and flowing numbers - then said I, "the bitterness is over past, for who can utter Melody in his sadness, or sing tunably when he is in a Strange land?" Since therefore the matter and the manner doe not agree, I also will sing:
"As men by storms may to their Haven Sail,
So let your Numbers, not your Sense prevail."
London, 25th X br 1686.

Wee have not seen Neddy these 3 weeks and therefore suppose him to bee with you. If hee had called here, I would have given him the hints you desired; although in truth it is not necessary, for I do not know what is what, and my own cake, whereof I thought to have given you a Bit, may prove dough. I have had a letter from Sir George Curtis, but can say to you little about it as yet. My observing the wind too much, makes me not sow.

But Cousin, the Bombs against my Essays are feared, one by La Republiq de Letters , and the other from the great Monsr Auzout from Rome. More are daily expected from Paris and particularly from the famous Abbot Bernou. I received Monsr Auzout's on Wensday last between 9 and 10, and carried the King an Answer before 12, made before all the White Staves in the Bed Chamber. The chief objection was, that the out-Parishes which have stood these 50 years in the Bills of Mortality, should not be accounted London. His paper did fall most upon what Captain Grant and myself had ever writ upon these matters.

I promised the King my speedy remarks upon all hee said, which I have since done and I hope pretty well. And afterwards I made 2 new Essays in one, where I proved over again all that I had said before of London, Rome, Roan and Dublin, even allowing Monsr Auzout all his Demands; even those for which hee had offered no manner of proof.

In the other Essays, wherein I deal with less favour and more Justice towards the Interest of Paris and Monsr Auzout, I show London to bee equal to Paris, Rome, and Roan, from their own sayings, although I do not believe it myself; which things I intend to show the King tomorrow if I can. I also, in answer to their objecting a City in Persia to bee
greater than London, show that (by their own sayings) the said Persian City had 44000 Moschees in it before Mahomet was come.
This do they get who wrong your poor Cousin, who wishes you a Merry Christmas, and that the next year may bee no worse than the past, and who is your good Company's and Kings-Weston and your own
honest servant.
Dear Cousin

Yours of the 25th past made our Christmas here look like it self, and we were all rejoycd to hear how you repelld the Roman Giant and got his Majesty of your side. When all is settled that relates to this predicament, I hope I shall not be the last to solemnise your fame, if you will but give me the means.
Neddy is with us and preparing his mind to pass a little time in Oxford. My Lady Percivale lately lost her only daughter by convultion fits, but the 3 boys doe bravely.

I see how cautious you are in Joining issue with Sir G. Curtis, and who can blame you? We are stunt on account of the same motives. What you think fit to spare as news or Information shall be looked on as from the hand it comes.
Doe you still think that the Parliament will here meet? I suppose their will soon be one in Ireland.

My Lady Dering prepares to be going up on Monday, and my Lady Percivale goes after, and they needs will have two of my girls of the party. I wish a happy year to my lady and to all yours, and am ever,
Yrs
Dear Cousin

I have yours of the 5th and thank you for the honour of It. All you write is to me a matter of Record. I could not conceal it from the Lord I am with, nor he forbear to desire an extract of it, so authentic it was in matter of moment and so entertaining in all the Rest.
I deplore the ejectments you mention and it drives me to remember a dirty rime imputed to Cromwell when they told him of Magna Charta.

My lady has my best wishes whether she goes or stays, and to make them stick I would fasten them with golden pins if I had them. My daughters brag of her ladyships favour towards them, and if my God-son take a stride into the world to enable him (in your own phrase) to 'live among dangerous men', may he prosper like his father's Bee Hive and return home again Crura thymo Plane .

You have so anatomized the wooden head, that I shall never mind it more, but for an echo, I wish you had heard one which the Lord Carlinford cairyed me to see within a mile of Milan. We stood in the gallery of a Gentleman's House, one story high, and in his garden (where were Trenches and I think some
standing water), the echo repeated after me the word "Home" 21 times distinctly.

I thank you for all the proportions of Land you mention. The reason of my enquiry herein was to enable me to Answer those who rashly affirm (and that in print) that the Irish had nothing by the Settlement; that if by the Usurper they were whipped with Iron, it has been since the Restoration with Scorpions.

What you add beyond what I requested, which is the Compromise of the 6 July 1665, is what I have long had in my Head, which you now diffinitly explain. I doe believe, and I think remember, that this Agreement was signed at my Lord Anglesey's House in Drury Lane, where the Lord Clancarty, Sir Nicholas Plunkett and the Heads of the Party did meet and agree thereto. I cannot say I saw the Paper, but I remember it was reported in Council that all was Agreed. And when in 1672 the Commission of Enquiry was on foot and Sir Henage Finch acted his part as a Champion for the Settlement, He so vigorously insisted on this Agreement that I remember the good King said in Council, "Nay I doe well remember there was some kind of agreement in this matter".

It seems this Paper is now lost or buried with these proceedings - which I once received from Sir James Shaen all in a deal Box; and for want of other Room, they were placed under the great Table in the Council Chamber and I believe remained there till the Chamber was lately altered. And who knows but it may still be found in the same box - if it be not a crime to look for it. As to my having Studied the several Peaces, it was purely to find by those Sibill's Books what might now ensue (at the least). For that which was once contended for with sword in hand, will now certainly be taken when it may be
had without contention. And what the moddell will be, is now I think the expectation of every Post.

I see how you have laid by the mala stamina of a History that was Intended, and what you say of Sir John Davys his Essays, and the misfortune of his Law and learning, which only enabled him to putt the Patch beside the Hole. If I live to see you I hope to be happier than the world, and see those treasures De Jure Belli, Jure Nature and Jure Gentium .
I return home in 3 days.
Piccadilly, 7 April 1687

The book (which you say might have been a Cartload) had 2 points in it: the one about the
Plague, the other about the new Wall propounded for London. Nobody but yourself hath taken notice of the former, and nobody at all of the latter - So deaf are the Adders wee charm unto!
As for the Settlement, Let us fancy it to bee a Ship and to be repaired and made better.
1o. The Coventry letter' propounds to break it up, burn most of the materials, and build some other Thing (not another Ship) with the rest.

2o. I meet with another who advises the sawing of it in 2 and making it longer, as also taking down her Upper-workes wherewith she is top-heavy, "for so" saith Hee "She will be a bigger and a better ship" - but Wee have not Carpenters to do it.
3o. The letter of the 15 November (which I praise and admire) thinks That calking it anew, and phay-goodling it almost, may serve turn.

4o. But I lately met with an old Carpenter sitting upon a Log of Timber, smoking his short pipe, to whom I said: "Do ye see that Ship yonder in the road?" - "See her" said hee, "A pox on her! I remember when she was built, and wrought myself for a while upon her, till I found knavery among the Chief owners and the workmen too, by Gad." - "Well" said I, "What do ye think of her?" - "Shoe's a rotten Toad" quoth hee, "There was a Cousin of the owner's that served us in rotten Timber and plank, which as it was laid was tarred over and looked like sufficient stuff, and the Devil and all." - "But do ye think she may bee mended?" - "Never" says hee, "without bringing her into a dry dock and taking out these planks and some of her principal timbers. Nay, a piece of her keel, by Gad." I intended to talk on with this Waspish Nimps but we were interrupted &c.

Within 2 days I met with Mr Houblon of whom I inquired concerning this Choleric old Coxcomb. But Mr Houblon said: "Hee is not so choleric as one would think, but having been horribly abused in and about that very ship. If you name 3 or 4 words
('Column' is one, the other 2 I can send you) Hee will, like Dol Common in the 'Alchemist', fall into Extravagances. Otherwise he is sober enough." "May be so", quoth I, "for though I got into the 'Anchor' I could not make him drink above a glass or 2." - Thus ends the parable &c.
To conclude. I find That if wee had a dry dock, These few timbers might bee mended without prejudice even to the mold of the present Hull.
20 april 1687
Dear Cousin

I had the honour of yours of the 7th and have much considerd the Parable of the Ship and your wishes for a dry dock. If a new draft were made, and every one certainly knew what would be done in this dock, and that the majority saw hopes of a Saving Voyage, the thoughts and votes and wishes of the powerful might run one way. But if a Chipp be touched without some such preamble, every plank will groan and expect to be flung into the fire.

The Coventry letter' runs now about in every hand on the other side, and gives terror as I am told; tho the Proclamation there, and the later declaration here, seem (as to Property) to Speak better things.

I am glad I animadverted on that piece of Angelic virtue in your Essay of limiting the Plague . It was new to me, and a blessing to mankind which I could not but admire. But for the other point of the London Wall , I had heard you speak of it before, so it was not altogether new. Nor am I martial man enough to take all things in that appertain to such a proposal. But we have a Martial King,
who hears you patiently, and might putt you to It. And I wonder He or his Lieutenant Generals doe not discuss this great point; as also an other you have in store, touching a defence by wool packs, applicable to land and sea.
My friend Monsieur Renaudot is ambitious to wait upon you. He is, among other Ingredients of ability, a good Geometrician; therefore pray smile upon him.
To my lady and the little ones all happiness.
Yrs
Kingsweston - 21 May 1687
Dear Cousin

The last post brought me, in yours of the 17th, a most unwelcome account of damage to your nephew and of approaching danger to your self. I see the Juries are set upon it, and every man must look about; since in this trial there was no defect in any circumstance or essential thing, but singly in the verdict. As for the scramble in Kerry, I see and admire your philosophy that you name it with patience. Before, you were lancd and scarified; but this is plain fleeing off the whole skin. But have the philosophy, and the same patience must also take place.

My present care is to save my stake at Kinsale by getting (if I can) a proviso in the new Charter that must follow the destruction of the old, and in which tic expected that all old members may be laid by. I am herein solicitous for the future, since at
present I can get no rent from thence. The town is become a poor skeleton, for all the trade is now centred in Cork - and tic high time that your friend Neddy doe hasten to the Law.
We are well in this place, as I hope it is with my lady and the little ones.

I have been writing a close sheet to Peter Welch in which you are often named. Tic on that part of his letter to the Bishop of Lincoln (p. 224) where he speaks of the Irish Rebellion and extenuates the first Massacre, and I think by the headings of your calculations I have the better of him.
Our Neddy is now got into Ethics. I am ever Yrs.
R. S.
I rejoice however that your nephew Nipper did behave himself so like a man in the day of battle. I remember well since his Father sweat for it in the Court of Claims, till all his hand was wet.
11 June 1687
Dear Cousin

This being the longest day in the year, I could wish it were Employed from morning to night in reading or writing like orders in your favour with
what you had on the 2nd from the Treasury; And tic most kindly done to send me the Copy of it. If my Lord Godolphin would now take consideration of what Sir Edward Dering Intended, I am able to give a large Testimonial of his being strangely convinced of your hard usage; and that he resolved to intercede not only for a full settlement in your affairs, but to the abating one hundred pounds per annum of the Quit Rents which you submitted unto - which in truth you did at his persuasion - I mean as regards concerns in Kerry.
What you apprehend of Shocks and disorders in other parts, I can but deplore, and employ wishes that it were otherwise than you find.

I have a great share of disappointment in my own small concerns, scarce getting any Rent at all, and I am menaced by the Courcys with trouble and law suites for having what their Ancestors, they say, had no right to dispose of. And this is the gratitude I find for respects to that poor family for near 40, or rather 50 years past, from my Father and my self. I suppose tic because they think witnesses and Juries can now doe any thing!
I see my Godson is going to the Academy, which I very well approve of, as also the disposal of my Cousin Harry.

If you can lend the answer of ten Sheets to Phillip Madox, he will presently get it copied out for me, and sent by a safe hand. I see you expect a broadside from Holland, but you have 18 Cities already for you, and so need not tremble before the Thunderbolt falls. I am apt to think they will consider well before they shoot, or repent their shooting.

I perceive you have been hearing of exercises at a School, which you think to be a sort of Music meeting, and that there may be Euphoniacall Nonsense.
I confess tic happiest when there is more care for the matter than the manner, tho this last is much easier sought for. As to the other it is Donum Dei , and you know to whom it was said at Merton College "Young man you were borne with 3 quarters of what you know".
Having named this college, I must not omit to tell you that Neddy does well according to the discipline of the place. He is already turned disputant in the Hall.

As you thrive by the order of the 2nd (that seems to show a certainty made in the present Rent, and in the Arrears) pray let me know it, as of all other things whether to profitt or loss - for when I cannot rejoice with you I will morn.
Yrs
8 July 1687
Dear Cousin

Since my acknowledgement of yours of the 16th past I have received and Read the papers, and doe think I never was better entertained in my life. I could say many things of so excellent a discourse, but will Comprise all in the words of Seneca, speaking of the Law: Non Irascitur sed Castigate . The 4th point which you thought wanting (being part of the Journal of the Supreme Council) is there as well as the rest, and serves as voucher in some particulars of the preceding discourse.

I am told from an Intelligent hand, as if there were hopes the Settlement would not be shaken, what ever is done with the Charters. And surely if those who have power, and no passion, did but read and consider your discourse (as perhaps they have done), they must be convinced that the Settlement cannot be broken without strange confusion in all his Majesty's affairs in the Kingdom.

But I hear of 11 Lords whose Outlawryes are discharged, and surely this looks not only as the
forerunner of a Parlyment, but as some assurance to them of having estates to support the dignity of Peerage.
You say nothing as yett of what has happened about Tecrohan, and your silence is a very good sign.
The late dissolution makes my hopes of seeing you very remote, and this not only in love to the Country, but as being on ground; for of ten letters from the other side, there is not one Bill.

My most humble service to my lady and the little ones. I have been reading this day "the Hind and Panther Transversed" and doe fancy none could make more of it than my Cousin Charles, for he would reach all the good humours that are in it.
I am always Yrs
Piccadilly, 4o Aug 1687
Charles was well at Rotterdam the 29th, but was 4 times 24 hours at sea.
I send you the Contents of the discourse I mentioned. I intend it to bee The Bible for Ireland. I have shown it in parts to some great Men, but not yet to the King; but will shortly.

The Customs of Dublin have, in this last quarter, fallen from 4 to 3, and the Excise from 7 to 6. Now although it hath been said with a loud voice That the people of Dublin are half run away (and by good observers that 1100 houses are void) Yet your Cousin assures you that in the last quarters hee finds more burials and Christnings than in any of the 10 quarters before. And therefore says that The people do retrench their expense in strong drink by 1/6 part and also in their housing, by crowding 7 families into 6 houses;
for 1100 is the 1/6 part of the houses in Dublin. The fall of lands appears to me by the fall of the Price of butter, Cheese, Milk, eggs, flesh, &c.
Adieu
Kingsweston, 13 Augt 1687
Dear Cousin

I have yours of the 4th and have read the papers enclosed, which are either for transplanting or Propagation. The things are mighty, and call unto my mind that when Paul reasoned of Righteousness, Temperance, and Judgement to come, Felix trembled. You know Columbus made the first offer to us of his Golden World, and was rejected; That the Sybill's Books, tho never so true, were undervalued; and Mr Newton's demonstrations will hardly be understood. The market rule goes fair in everything else, Tantum valet quantum vent potest . So as tho I doe not suspect you can be mistaken in what you assert, since you enumerate so many solid as well as bitter objections thereunto; yett the dullness of the world is such, the opposers so many, your fellow labourers so few, and your Age so advanced, that I reckon the work Insuperable. However I am glad that your thoughts are all written down, for Posterity, as favoured by great Accidents, may cultivate what the present Age neglects. And in the mean time since you propose to entertain the King on these subjects, let me advertise you what his good Brother once said at The Council Board - That he thought you one of the best Commissioners of the Navy that ever was; That you had vast knowledge in many things - "But" said he "the man will not be contented to be excellent, but is still Aiming at Impossible Things".

You know I am in possession of saying any thing to you that comes in my head; but this I say for your service, that being already advanced in
his Majesty's opinion for things that he Comprehends, you doe not grow less by going beyond his Reach.

I rejoice to hear that Cousin Charles got safe, tho after good tossing, to the other side. Your letters will not be less welcome if you sprinkle them with a little good tidings of him and of his Improvements. I say the same for the rest, and am ever
Yrs
Pray Cousin, did you ever use any Art to Improve your memory? Tully De oratore uses many words to show how it may be Improved by Images, but I desire your saying.
Kingsweston, 28 Sept. 1687
Dear Cousin

Upon a fresh Review of your letter of the 16th past, the particulars are of that Bulk and importance and my digestion so incompetent, that
I must swear, as the honest Recusant did of Queen Elizabeth, That 'if she was not the Head of the Church, he wished she were soe'.

But first as to my Cousin Charles. I see you resign him to the impression of his Stars. And as one Tree will not become another, or oaks and Cedars much alter their Shape, so you will allow that withyes are to be twisted towards what one would have them to be, and dead wood must by Carving be brought into Figure. And, it standing thus between your son and mine, perhaps we are both in the right!

I perceive you have tried the Artificial Memory and undervalue It. If the Ancient Orators had it with advantage and for use, It seems their method is Lost. The Chief Rule we now have left is only exercise and conning of things overnight. But if you know better, I will ask questions herein at your coming down. You must then also expect I shall be very importunate to see the 20 Articles which contain the Weight of the Crown , which you presented his Majesty - and certainly with the most peculiar Test I ever heard, viz: to pick out any one He wished to be true, and any other He suspected to be false, and that in 24 hours He should have demonstration. But tho you complain that after all that you got neither Butter or Hobb-nayles hereby, yett you fare much better than He who found out the Malleable Glass.

You doubtless touch a very sore place when you suspect the surviving malice of the Double ship. Your fate compared herein to that of Action's goes very far, as having courted the King's Mysteries. Yett I may say that if this last word should be mistaken for 'Mistresses', then to have had a fresh one and of your procurement, as well as of any others, sounds
not as a matter that should have turned to your disadvantage!

Your observation of the Poverty that is already grown, and must ensue while mouths increase and yett eating grows less, is so much more a valuable stroke in your Art of Calculation as it is seen felt and understood by all. And doubtelesse the other great things you mention may be as Rationally founded, though unequally comprehended. And I confess unto you that, tho the world should never be wise enough to wed what you propose in the Multiplication of Men and the benefits flowing from it, yett if you have as strong motives for the Truth of these matters as usually convince men from the Pulpit or at the Barr, I cannot wonder that you are Ravished with the harmony and charms of Ratiocination. You very well call it a Labour of Pleasure', but not so properly 'Angelicall', since tic perhaps the only pleasure the angels want. For Intuition of truth may not Relish so much as Truth that is hunted down.

But if you intend Pyramids out of these materials to bear testimony of your good will to mankind, when you pass to a better life, you should take care while you are among us to explain all and leave as few Hieroglyphics as is possible. And I, if I live, will not fail to assist my Godson to hand them to the Press. Tho doubtless it were better done while you are yett on this side the pitt.

You see how little I can say to those mighty things you honour me withal; But I keep them Charily together, and my son may find Charms where I now Languish. He is now with me and to stay all the winter; since Oxford is already, and is growing more, an unquiet place.
I am ever Yrs
R. S.
Kingsweston, 10 Oct 1687
Dear Cousin

Yours of the 4th came to me the next day after I had sent you some lincks of very Saucy but friendly thoughts. As to your Purchase, I here send you what the Surveyor answers. He is a plain frugal man. And as to instructing Mr Plumbly, I
think what you said goes through the whole Alphabet, nor doe I think that ever such a Scheme was made before. I cannot yett find where to wedge in a word, but I will try when tic fair weather, for now I am very dull.

If you lay out but 2500£, it must be in Revertions for your Grandson and when the Tenements are full Stated. Our Neddy read these Instructions with marvellous relish, which is some sign he may get them into his head; but he is just now as hot as mustard upon Logic and proposed to me to write his thoughts to Cousin Charles on that dry Subject. I told him Charles might show it his father, and so he might burn his fingers. At last being earnest I let him take his cource, for the exercise may doe him good though Charles has better things to mind. I wish however that Charles would urge him to write 20 letters more on the several parts of this doctrine, for perhaps the being made accountable may doe him some good.
The ill weather putts me out of humour to write more at present, than that I am Yrs
R. S.
Kingsweston, 16th December 1687
Dear Cousin

I was yesterday in some fright upon reading from Phillip Madox the report of your sickness, but the favour of yours of the 13th dispelld the cloud, as making slight of the matter. However it will be very welcome to me to hear that you walk again as you did before.
I see and congratulate that you have been able to lay so great a Tanto at the Farmours doors, and that you are hastening to make even with all others.

As for the demand of 7774£ 10s-, which yett (as you say) is not half the wrong you have suffered, and of which you shall never willingly abate - the figure I hold between my Friend and Patron, as well as ignorance in the particular merits of the case,
makes it fit for me above all other to be silent; and I can assure you that if the old Gentleman had half such a demand from you, I would not be his Herald tho he should desire it. Things of anger and the prospect of war (in a warm attic and as warm a defence) drives the Common friend into a corner; and he steps not out till he finds both convinced in their Hearts that it were their Common Interest to be quiet. From these Motives, and because you also leave me to do what I will with the paper, I will keep it to myself; and the rather because I rarely hear from him since the gout has disabled him, and as seldom write.

Even you who are the Claymer, seem tenderly to wish that you had nothing but poses to toss against him, and I am sure I do as cordially wish that at this time of day, and while both are in the storm, there were nothing but sweet odours, as the tossing of Incense, between you.
With all true service to my Lady and little ones,
I am ever yrs
R. S.
